attribution.note: Marcus's own postscript in his post, reporting his own Bing test.

semantics.note: Keeps his words '4/4' and 'completely flubbed' for the prompt he quoted. It is a past observation of his own test.

contract.note: Reading Bing as its image generator and taking July 2024 as the period is an ordinary reading. The contract rightly needs an independent record of the four outputs.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no evidence items. The only record is the speaker's own screenshot, which cannot prove itself. Image outputs are random and the model has changed since 2024, so the test cannot be replicated faithfully. Nothing available settles whether all four images failed.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence. The quotes of Bjarnason and Upwork nearby are separate.

semantics.note: 'May' hedges only the concession about coders. The main clause, 'much of the outside world feels quite differently', is firm. 'Many workers' is a fair stand-in for 'much of the outside world' in a post about work.

contract.note: 'Much of' read as a large minority, calendar 2024, and general worker surveys are ordinary readings. Counting generative AI broadly as ChatGPT is a slight stretch but fits the context.

evidence.note: Upwork survey from April-May 2024: 77% of employees using AI say it added to their workload. Upwork published it, but it is a survey of workers, not a claim about Upwork, and the contract names it as an accepted source.
Pew, October 2024: most chatbot users did not rate the tools as highly helpful for speed (60%) or for quality (71%). Published before the evaluation date.
Pew: 69% of workers don't use chatbots at work, and 36% of those see no use for them in their job. That is about a quarter of all workers, showing wide indifference.
Regular users often found chatbots highly helpful. This tempers the claim but falls well short of the contract's bar of broad majority enthusiasm, so it does not contradict.

reviews.rationale: Credible 2024 surveys show large shares of workers found generative AI added work, was not very helpful, or had no use in their job. That meets the support condition. There is no evidence of broad majority enthusiasm. Caveats: neither survey separates out coders, and they cover generative AI in general, not ChatGPT alone.
